KEY MESSAGE 1...Latest surface analysis this afternoon shows a 
shallow but well saturated layer ahead of a strong cold front 
working its way across the Appalachians, driven by a strong 
shortwave diving out of the Great Lakes. Until the front comes 
through and scours out the low level moisture, conditions will 
remain partly to mostly cloudy. Given some very weak ascent 
ahead of the front cannot rule out a shallow shower or two 
contributing a couple hundredths of an inch.

Strong CAA will ramp up quickly behind the front with strong 
high pressure building and wedging in from the north. This will 
briefly lock in a cooler and drier airmass for Tuesday with 
breezier conditions as gusts top out around 20-25 mph inland and
up to 40 mph for some coastal sections. Temperatures fall back 
below average with highs struggling to reach 60 and lows down in
the upper 30s inland.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Pattern quickly gets complex by mid-week as a 
potent sub-tropical jet will remain in place through the week. A
strong upper level trough currently working its way into the 
Four Corners region will ride this jet, tracking eastward into 
the Plains. Finally, an upper low is forecast to deepen and dive
southeastward out of the Canadian prairies and tracks towards 
the Ohio River Valley. The latter two features will undergo a 
complex interaction over the eastern CONUS, with the Plains 
trough digging further into the Gulf Coast and taking on a 
negative tilt as it interactions of the OH Valley low. We will 
see a similar evolution at the mid-levels with two potent 
shortwave troughs.

This overall pattern favors surface cyclogenesis along the 
Southeastern coast, although how the aforementioned features 
interact will play a large role in the low's track and 
intensity. These remain open questions given ongoing spread 
among Euro and GEFS ensembles. However, the trend from yesterday
continues to move towards a stronger and potentially 
significant low impacting the region as early as tomorrow night 
but most likely Wednesday into Thursday.

As the low tracks northeast and deepens as it moves towards the
Carolinas, it will begin to buttress the surface high still 
wedged over the mid-Atlantic. The resulting pressure gradient 
will bring strong winds to the region, peaking Wed night into 
Thursday and most acutely felt over the Outer Banks with gusts 
up to 50 mph at times. Gusts up to 30 mph are also possible 
inland. This is a shift upwards from the previous forecast and 
would necessitate wind-related headlines either tonight or 
tomorrow for at least the Outer Banks. The higher winds also 
heightens concerns for coastal flooding...see KEY MESSAGE 3 for 
more details on this.

The low will also pull up a plume of very deep moisture from 
the Atlantic with PWATs forecast to exceed 2" (per climatology 
this is roughly 300%+ of normal for late November). With the 
strong ascent aloft, heavy rainfall is likely. The low track 
will determine the axis of heaviest rainfall, but all of eastern
NC has a 70-80% chance of seeing at least 2 inches of rain 
focused around Wed night into Thursday. Areas focused along NC24
and the Outer Banks south of Hatteras are most favored for 
higher amounts with a probability of exceeding 4" at 40-50% 
(less than 20% farther inland). Even with the area in portions 
of severe to extreme drought, this level of rainfall could still
pose a threat of flash flooding across the area especially in 
urban corridors.

KEY MESSAGE 3...ENC is currently experiencing the next round of
king tides this week with an increase in antecedant water 
levels. These are expected to peak on Wednesday and then quickly
fall off by Friday, and will be slightly higher than the cycle 
that occurred in October. The tide alone will act to pile up 
water especially soundside in the Pamlico Sound, Neuse River and
adjacent areas. This could lead to some minor water rises 
tomorrow across both sound- and ocean-side locations along the 
Outer Banks, as well as the Neuse River.

The mid-week storm, in combination with the tides, will 
exacerbate water level and coastal flooding concerns. Most tidal
locations across ENC are likely to see at least minor to 
moderate impacts, with the risk for more significant impacts for
more typically vulnerable locations given forecast gusts of up 
to 40-50 mph. Interests along the coast should continue to 
closely monitor forecasts through the week.
